query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Premelting and melting behavior in FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by a competition between nanoscale surface segregation of the low–melting-point element (copper) and the entropic stabilization of a homogeneous solid solution. This leads to the formation of a thin, compositionally enriched liquid-like (premelted) surface layer at temperatures below the bulk melting point, which then propagates into the particle core as the temperature increases.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, single-phase FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with a homogeneous chemical composition as synthesized by high-temperature synthesis techniques.
generation.intervention: Subject nanoparticles to controlled in situ heating (e.g., via TEM heating stage or differential scanning calorimetry with simultaneous high-resolution spatial compositional analysis) to monitor the onset and progression of premelting and melting. A controlled comparison is made between the standard HEA nanoparticles and either bimetallic particles of similar size or HEA nanoparticles processed to minimize elemental segregation.
generation.conditions: Experiments should be conducted in a high-vacuum or inert-gas environment to avoid oxidation, with precise temperature control spanning from near the anticipated premelting onset (possibly around 0.8–0.9 times the aggregate melting temperature) to complete melting. The heating rate should be slow enough to resolve the phase-transition progression and permit real-time EDS or similar compositional mapping.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a superficial layer enriched in copper (as well as possibly other slight local compositional deviations induced by elemental size mismatch and differing surface energies) acts as the structural mediator. This layer lowers the local melting temperature relative to the interior, setting up a gradient from a liquid-like disordered surface to an ordered solid core.
generation.mechanism: Due to differences in melting points and surface energies among the constituent elements (with Cu being the lowest), copper atoms preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface at elevated temperatures. This segregation reduces the local melting temperature at the surface, resulting in early (premelting) formation of a liquid or disordered surface layer. As temperature increases, this premelting layer grows inward; however, the high configurational entropy stabilizes the internal solid solution, delaying complete melting until a critical thickness or degree of segregation is reached.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline case (e.g., single-metal nanoparticles or chemically simpler bimetallic nanoparticles), FeNiCrCoCu HEA nanoparticles will show a two‐stage melting behavior: an initial premelting stage characterized by the appearance of a thin, copper-enriched, liquid-like surface layer at a temperature significantly below the bulk melting temperature, followed by a gradual propagation of melting towards the core as temperature increases. The onset of premelting (temperature and layer thickness) should be measurably lower or more gradual than in the baseline heterogeneous systems.
generation.baseline: The baseline is nanoparticles with similar size and geometry but either single-metal composition (where premelting is driven solely by surface curvature effects) or less chemically complex bimetallic particles that do not exhibit significant elemental segregation effects.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies primarily to nanoparticles in which the high surface-to-volume ratio accentuates elemental segregation phenomena. It is expected to hold within the temperature regime from approximately 0.8T_m (where T_m is the averaged bulk melting temperature of the HEA) to complete melting, and for particles where diffusion kinetics allow for mild segregation within the experimental time scale. Larger particles or systems with slower diffusion kinetics may not display the same pronounced premelting behavior.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the quantitative extent of copper segregation and the exact temperature range over which the premelting layer forms, as well as the interplay with potential rapid interdiffusion that could maintain compositional homogeneity. The size effect and specific synthesis history may also influence the observed behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform an in situ heating experiment with high-resolution TEM coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to monitor both the structural and compositional changes as a function of temperature. Compare the onset of the liquid-like, disordered surface layer and its copper enrichment in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles to that in control nanoparticles (e.g., single-metal or less complex bimetallic systems) under identical heating conditions.
measurements: Temperature-dependent imaging to detect the formation and propagation of a premelted layer.
EDS compositional profiling across the nanoparticle radius to determine if copper enrichment occurs at the surface during premelting.
Calorimetric measurements (e.g., DSC) to quantify the onset temperature of the premelting and complete melting events.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ measurements do not show the formation of an early, copper-enriched premelted surface layer (i.e., the onset of melting is uniform across the nanoparticle or matches that of baseline single-metal systems) or if the compositional profiles remain uniform throughout heating, then the hypothesis is rejected.
